extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in philosophy, history, and sociology of science; practicing scientists interested in theory-change and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing the nature, components, and consequences of scientific paradigms and community structure for theory change, normal science, and revolutions. Focuses on how groups share commitments (the 'disciplinary matrix') and how that shapes research, crises, and paradigm shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm as constellation of group commitments (disciplinary matrix)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm (better: a 'disciplinary matrix') consists of the entire constellation of beliefs, values, techniques, and so on shared by the members of a scientific community — ordered elements of various sorts which form a functioning whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components should be disentangled analytically rather than treated as a single undifferentiated entity. The disciplinary matrix approach clarifies what group members share and how those shared elements enable professional communication and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm as exemplary past achievements (exemplars/puzzle-solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigm in the narrower sense denotes concrete puzzle-solutions — exemplary past achievements — which, employed as models or examples, can replace explicit rules as a basis for solving remaining puzzles of normal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sense is philosophically deeper: exemplars function as models that guide problem solving and are central to the habituated practice of normal science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic generalizations are expressions deployed without question by group members and readily cast in logical form (e.g., f = ma or I = V/R); they are the formal or readily formalizable components of the disciplinary matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They function both as laws and in part as definitions of the symbols they use. Their balance between legislative and definitional force shifts over time; acceptance may require redefining terms and can provoke resistance (e.g., Ohm’s Law episode). The power of a science tends to increase with the number of such generalizations available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models (heuristic and ontological)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared commitments to particular models — including heuristic models (e.g., electric circuit as hydrodynamic analogue) and ontological models (e.g., atoms, fields) — are constituents of the disciplinary matrix and serve to supply preferred analogies and metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models help determine what is accepted as explanation, which puzzles are posed, and evaluations of puzzle importance. Strength of commitment to models varies; membership in a community may not always require belief in a given model (e.g., early 19th-century chemists and atoms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Values guiding theory appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared values include: predictions should be accurate; quantitative predictions are preferable to qualitative; margins of permissible error should be consistently satisfied; theories must permit puzzle-formulation and solution; they should be simple, self-consistent, plausible, and compatible with other current theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values are widely shared but their application varies by individual; values are central when identifying crises or choosing between incompatible approaches. Attention to internal and external consistency is important for analyzing crisis sources and theory choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared values applied variably (role of personality and distribution of risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though values are widely held, individual scientists often apply them differently; different values taken alone can dictate different theory choices (e.g., accuracy vs plausibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variable application can be functional: it distributes risk in the community (some take high-risk departures, others conserve), enabling both stability and the possibility of revolutionary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community structure as primary unit of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific communities consist of practitioners of a specialty who have undergone similar training, absorbed the same literature, and share responsibility for pursuing shared goals; paradigms govern groups of practitioners rather than abstract subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communities can be identified by subject of highest degree, professional society membership, journals read, attendance at special conferences, distribution of draft manuscripts, correspondence networks, and citation linkages. Analysis of paradigm-directed research must begin by locating the responsible group(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels and sizes of scientific communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities exist at multiple levels (global natural scientists, major professions like physicists, narrower subgroups, and small specialty groups). Typical contemporary communities may be on the order of ~100 members, sometimes fewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists may belong to multiple communities. Identifying communities at different scales matters for understanding when changes are revolutionary within a group though small from a broader perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition from pre-paradigm to post-paradigm periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition reduces competing schools (pre-paradigm multiplicity) to fewer or one dominant school (post-paradigm) enabling an efficient, esoteric, puzzle-solving mode of normal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquisition of the sort of paradigm that identifies challenging puzzles and supplies clues allows normal science to proceed. This transition need not coincide with the first appearance of paradigm-like elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis as usual prelude (but not necessary) to revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Crises — a common awareness that something has gone wrong — are typically the prelude to revolutions, supplying a self-correcting mechanism that prevents rigidity of normal science from persisting indefinitely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crises are not absolute prerequisites; revolutions may be induced in other ways and crises affecting one community may be generated by developments (instruments, laws) in another specialty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm governs practitioners not fixed subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm governs a group of practitioners; subject matters have shifted historically across different communities (e.g., 'physics' formed from earlier mathematics and natural philosophy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore historical and analytic work must unravel changing community structures over time; treating paradigms as identical to subject matters can produce misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions involve redefinition/abandonment of previously tautological generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many revolutions involve abandoning generalizations whose force had partly been tautological (definitions); revolutions can thus alter the meanings of key terms (e.g., simultaneity) as well as what counts as law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some symbolic generalizations serve definitional as well as law-like functions, their replacement can require reconceptualization of core terms — a locus of resistance and paradox in theory change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular definition of paradigm/community (method for paradigm discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not define a paradigm circularly as 'what members of a community share' while defining community as 'those who share a paradigm.' Instead, isolate communities by empirical techniques and then discover paradigms by scrutinizing their behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical techniques include bibliometrics, conference attendance, manuscript distribution, and analysis of communication networks; this avoids vicious circularity and yields usable analytic units for study.
